# Set up a shared private LEZ account

#### Get started with group-owned private accounts where every member independently derives the same keys.

> **Tip: Version**
>
> This document is accurate for **Testnet v0.3.0**.

This procedure covers how to create a shared [private account](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#private-account) (regular or [PDA](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#pda)) on the [LEZ](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#lez) that is jointly controlled by multiple members. From one 32-byte [Group Master Secret](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#group-master-secret) ([GMS](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#gms)), every member independently derives the same [account](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#account) keys ([NSK](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#nsk), [VSK](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#vsk), [NPK](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#npk), [VPK](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#vpk)), so any member can view and spend the shared balance without an interactive key exchange at spend time. It is intended for developers on testnet v0.3 who need multi-party custody of a private balance or a private PDA.

This feature is 1-of-n at the key layer: any GMS holder can derive every key and spend the account. Threshold gating must be implemented at the [program](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#program) layer. View-only membership is not supported—any GMS holder gets both viewing and spending capability.

> **Info: Prerequisites**
>
>
> - A supported OS:
>    - Linux x86_64 or aarch64
>    - macOS arm64 or x86_64 (requires full Xcode with the Metal toolchain for the Risc0 guest build)
> - A local clone of the [LEZ repository](https://github.com/logos-blockchain/logos-execution-zone).
> - An [LEZ CLI wallet](https://docs.logos.co/lez/get-started/run-lez-wallet-via-cli.md) set up and funded.

## What to expect

- You can create a shared private account from a single GMS so that every invited member independently derives the same NPK, VPK, NSK, and VSK without an interactive key exchange at spend time. (Members must agree on the same PDA `--seed`, `--program-id`, and `--identifier` values; see Step 4.)
- You can admit new members by sealing the GMS to their sealing public key and having them unseal it locally, with no shared secrets transmitted in the clear.
- You can create a group-owned PDA family where each PDA is distinguished by an identifier derived from the same group keys.

## Step 1: Generate a sealing key pair for each member

Each member who will join a group needs a one-time [sealing key](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#sealing-keys) pair before the owner can invite them. The sealing key uses ML-KEM-768 and is kept separate from account [viewing keys](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#viewing-keys).

1. Each joining member generates their sealing key pair:

   ```sh
   wallet group new-sealing-key
   ```

   - This prints the sealing public key. Each member shares the public key with the group owner.
   - Run this once per wallet. The secret key is stored locally and never shared.
   - Save the printed public key. A wallet holds exactly one sealing key: running the command again
     returns `Error: Sealing key already exists`, and there is no command to print the existing
     public key again.

## Step 2: Create the group and the shared account

The group owner creates a local group with a fresh random GMS, then derives a shared account from it. Accounts derived from the same group with the same PDA parameters (`--seed`, `--program-id`, `--identifier`) have identical keys for every member who holds the GMS.

1. Create the group with a fresh random GMS:

   ```sh
   wallet group new test-group
   ```

   - The group is registered locally and visible in `wallet group list` (alias `ls`).

1. Create the shared account derived from the group. Use the PDA form and record the `--seed`, `--program-id`, and `--identifier` values—the other members need exactly these values in Step 4 to derive the same account:

   ```sh
   wallet account new private-gms test-group --pda \
     --seed <32-byte-hex> --program-id <program-id-hex> --identifier 0 --label shared-acc
   ```

   `--identifier` diversifies one PDA from another within the same `(program_id, seed)` family; it defaults to a random value if omitted, so set it explicitly for a shared account.

   - The plain form creates a regular private account owned by this wallet alone:

     ```sh
     wallet account new private-gms test-group --label shared-acc
     ```

     It derives with a fresh random identifier on every invocation, so other members running the same command land on different accounts. Use it only when you do not need the account to be reproducible by other GMS holders.

## Step 3: Invite a new member by sealing the GMS

The owner seals the GMS to each new member's sealing public key using ML-KEM-768. The sealed GMS is safe to transmit over any channel.

1. Seal the group's GMS for the new member using their sealing public key:

   ```sh
   wallet group invite test-group --key <joining-member-sealing-pubkey-hex>
   ```

   - Share this hex string with the new member over any channel. Repeat this step for each additional member.

## Step 4: Join the group and derive the shared account

The new member unseals the GMS using their local sealing secret key and derives their instance of the shared account. With the same PDA parameters the owner used, the derived keys are identical to those held by every other member.

1. Unseal the GMS and store it under a local group name:

   ```sh
   wallet group join my-copy --sealed <sealed-gms-hex-from-owner>
   ```

   - The GMS is now stored locally under `my-copy`. Both the owner and this member now hold the same GMS.

1. Derive the shared account from the joined group.

   > **Warning**
   >
   > For regular (non-PDA) shared accounts, each `wallet account new private-gms` invocation diversifies the derived keys with a random identifier, so running the plain command in two wallets produces two different accounts even from the same GMS. To land on the same account as the other members, use the PDA form with an agreed `--seed`, `--program-id`, and `--identifier`—with identical values, every GMS holder derives identical keys.

   ```sh
   wallet account new private-gms my-copy --pda \
     --seed <32-byte-hex> --program-id <program-id-hex> --identifier 0
   ```

   - With the same `--seed`, `--program-id`, and `--identifier` values as the owner used, this produces the same account ID, NPK, VPK, NSK, and VSK as the owner's account derived in Step 2.

---

> Source: https://docs.logos.co/lez/programs/write-and-deploy-lez-program-with-scaffold
> Markdown index of all Logos docs: https://docs.logos.co/llms.txt

# Write and deploy an LEZ program with `logos-scaffold`

#### Use `logos-scaffold` to create, build, and deploy a guest program on a local Logos Execution Zone sequencer.

> **Tip: Version**
>
> This document is accurate for `logos-scaffold` **0.4.0** built from `master` at commit `d4b15ff`, which pins LEZ **v0.1.2**. It deploys to a local sequencer only; see [Deploy to the testnet](#deploy-to-the-testnet).

[`logos-scaffold`](https://github.com/logos-co/scaffold) is a project scaffold and CLI tool that manages the full lifecycle of a [LEZ](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#lez) guest [program](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#program)—from project creation to deployment. It pins LEZ and SPEL dependencies, builds a project-local sequencer, and handles wallet interactions, so you can focus on writing your program logic.

This guide walks each stage separately so you can see what the tool does. Once the pieces are familiar, [`logos-scaffold run`](#use-logos-scaffold-run-for-the-inner-loop) chains them into a single command. For what else scaffold manages, including Basecamp modules, see [About Logos Scaffold](https://docs.logos.co/build-an-app/scaffold/about-logos-scaffold.md).

> **Info: Prerequisites**
>
>
> - A supported OS:
>     - Linux: x86_64
>     - macOS
> - `git`, and Rust 1.81 or newer with `cargo`.
> - The Unix process helpers `lsof`, `ps`, and `kill`, and `curl`.
> - The [RISC Zero toolchain](https://dev.risczero.com/api/zkvm/install), installed with `rzup`:
>
>     ```bash
>     curl -L https://risczero.com/install | bash   # installs rzup; restart your shell afterwards
>     rzup install rust
>     rzup install cargo-risczero 3.0.5
>     ```
>
>     `rust` builds the guest programs. `cargo-risczero` provides `r0vm`, which the sequencer needs to execute transactions, and it must be the version LEZ `v0.1.2` pins, `3.0.5`: scaffold only looks for that version, under `~/.risc0/extensions/`. Without it, `localnet start` still reports `localnet ready`, with a warning about `RISC0_SERVER_PATH`, and `deploy` then fails. If you installed `rzup` with a custom `RISC0_HOME`, export `RISC0_SERVER_PATH` with the full path to that `r0vm`.
> - [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/), with the daemon running. Scaffold builds guest programs inside the pinned `risczero/risc0-guest-builder` container by default, so that a `program_id` is the same on every machine. Without Docker, opt out as described in [Step 5](#step-5-build-the-project).
> - About 5 GB of free disk space for the pinned LEZ and `spel` builds.
>
> Nix is not needed for this guide, only for scaffold's `basecamp` commands. If it is not installed, `logos-scaffold doctor` reports a `tool nix` warning that you can ignore.

## What to expect

- You can create an LEZ program project and write a guest program that runs inside the RISC0 zkVM.
- You can build your program and deploy it to a project-local LEZ sequencer.
- You can call your deployed program and repeat the whole loop with one command.

## Step 1: Install logos-scaffold

1. Install the CLI from the scaffold repository, pinned to the commit this guide was tested with:

    ```bash
    cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/logos-co/scaffold --rev d4b15ff logos-scaffold
    ```

    This installs two binaries on your PATH: `logos-scaffold` and the shorter alias `lgs`. They are functionally identical. The `logos-scaffold` 0.4.0 release on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/logos-scaffold) predates the Docker guest build in [Step 5](#step-5-build-the-project), so `cargo install logos-scaffold` gives you a CLI without `--guest` and with guest artifacts in a different place.

1. Verify the installation:

    ```bash
    logos-scaffold --version
    ```

## Step 2: Create a new project

1. Create a new LEZ program project. Replace `my-program` with your project name:

    ```bash
    logos-scaffold new my-program
    cd my-program
    ```

    This generates a project with the `default` template, which includes sample guest programs and runner scripts. For an Anchor-style framework with IDL and generated client bindings, pass `--template lez-framework` instead; this guide follows the default template.

    > **Info**
    >
    > `new` also clones the pinned LEZ source into scaffold's shared cache; with the builds from [Step 3](#step-3-set-up-the-project) the cache grows to about 3.5 GB. To keep it somewhere else, pass `--cache-root <path>` or set `LOGOS_SCAFFOLD_CACHE_ROOT`.

1. Inspect the project layout:

    ```text
    my-program/
    ├── scaffold.toml          # Project configuration and dependency pins
    ├── methods/
    │   └── guest/
    │       └── src/bin/       # Guest programs run inside the RISC0 zkVM
    ├── src/
    │   └── bin/               # Runner scripts that submit transactions
    ├── AGENTS.md              # Guidance for AI coding assistants
    ├── .claude/skills/        # The same guidance for Claude Code
    ├── .cursor/rules/         # The same guidance for Cursor
    └── .scaffold/             # Local state, wallet home, and build artifacts
    ```

## Step 3: Set up the project

1. Run `setup` to sync the LEZ and SPEL repositories to their pinned commits, build the project-local sequencer and wallet binaries, and seed the default wallet:

    > **Warning**
    >
    > Scaffold unlocks the wallet it seeds with a deterministic local password, so the onboarding flow needs no prompts. To use your own, export it **before the first `setup`** (or the first `run`, which chains `setup`):
    >
    > ```bash
    > export LOGOS_SCAFFOLD_WALLET_PASSWORD='<your-local-dev-password>'
    > ```
    >
    > If the storage was already created under the default password, export the override and re-seed with `logos-scaffold run --reset`. These are development-only keys; never use them for real funds.

    ```bash
    logos-scaffold setup
    ```

    On a cold cache this step builds the sequencer, wallet, and `spel` from source, which takes about 20 minutes on a four-core machine. Later runs reuse the build.

1. Check the project's environment. `doctor` reports missing tools and configuration problems, with a next step for each:

    ```bash
    logos-scaffold doctor
    ```

    At this point expect three `WARN` rows about the sequencer, because the localnet is not running yet. [Step 6](#step-6-start-a-local-sequencer) clears them. A `FAIL` on the `guest build` row means `docker` or `cargo-risczero` is not on your `PATH`; see [Step 5](#step-5-build-the-project).

## Step 4: Write your guest program

Guest programs run inside the [RISC0 zkVM](https://dev.risczero.com/) and define the on-chain logic of your LEZ program. Each guest program in `methods/guest/src/bin/` becomes a deployable program with its own `program_id`.

1. Open the sample guest program:

    ```bash
    $EDITOR methods/guest/src/bin/hello_world.rs
    ```

1. Read how the program works. It receives a `ProgramInput` struct via the zkVM environment, applies your logic, and writes a `ProgramOutput` struct to the journal. The sequencer verifies the proof and updates the on-chain [account](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#account) state.

    Key concepts:
    - **Instructions** are passed as bytes. `hello_world` takes its instruction as a raw `Vec<u8>` and appends it to the account's data.
    - **Account data** is stored in `AccountWithMetadata` structs.
    - Use `RISC0_DEV_MODE=1` during development to skip ZK proof generation for faster iteration.

## Step 5: Build the project

1. Build the workspace. In development, use `RISC0_DEV_MODE=1` to skip proof generation:

    ```bash
    RISC0_DEV_MODE=1 logos-scaffold build
    ```

    The build compiles the workspace, then builds each guest program inside the pinned `risczero/risc0-guest-builder` Docker image and writes the `.bin` artifacts to `target/riscv-guest-docker/riscv32im-risc0-zkvm-elf/docker/`. The same source then produces the same bytes, and therefore the same `program_id`, on any machine. The first build takes several minutes.

    If the Docker daemon is not running, `build` stops straight away:

    ```text
    error: [build].guest = "docker" needs a running Docker daemon; `docker info` failed.
    ```

1. To build without Docker, use the host RISC Zero toolchain instead. For one build, pass `--guest local`:

    ```bash
    RISC0_DEV_MODE=1 logos-scaffold build --guest local
    ```

    To make it the project default, which [`logos-scaffold run`](#use-logos-scaffold-run-for-the-inner-loop) needs because it has no `--guest` flag, add this to `scaffold.toml`:

    ```toml
    [build]
    guest = "local"
    ```

    A local build writes the artifacts to `target/riscv-guest/…/riscv32im-risc0-zkvm-elf/release/` instead. Its `program_id` depends on your host's Rust and clang versions, so it can differ from the one another machine builds from the same source. Each `build` removes the other mode's artifacts, so `deploy` always ships the output of the last `build`. `logos-scaffold doctor` shows the active mode in its `guest build` row.

## Step 6: Start a local sequencer

1. Start a project-local sequencer to deploy your program to:

    ```bash
    RISC0_DEV_MODE=1 logos-scaffold localnet start
    ```

    `start` returns once the sequencer process is alive and its RPC port answers. The sequencer is daemonised and survives terminal or tmux session closure. Use `logos-scaffold localnet status` to check that it is running and `logos-scaffold localnet stop` to stop it.

    > **Warning**
    >
    > The local sequencer always uses port `3040`. If something else already listens there, such as another scaffold project's sequencer, `localnet start` fails with `Address already in use (os error 98)`, and `localnet status` reports `ownership: foreign`. Stop the other process first. Changing `port` under `[localnet]` in `scaffold.toml` does not help: the sequencer still binds `3040` and the wallet keeps pointing at it, so `deploy` and `wallet topup` would talk to the other sequencer.
    >
    > For any other failure, read the sequencer log with `logos-scaffold localnet logs --tail 200`. To wipe chain state and start over, run `logos-scaffold localnet reset --yes`.

## Step 7: Deploy your program

1. Deploy all guest programs to the running sequencer:

    ```bash
    RISC0_DEV_MODE=1 logos-scaffold deploy
    ```

    - After each successful submission, `logos-scaffold` prints `program_id: <hex>`, the RISC0 image ID computed locally from the submitted ELF. It prints `program_id: unavailable` if the project's `spel` binary has not been built yet. The example runner scripts in [Step 8](#step-8-interact-with-your-program) load the program from its embedded ELF, so you do not need to copy a `program_id` to complete this guide.
    - `deploy` checks that the sequencer is reachable before submitting, and stops with a hint if it is not. It submits one program per block, so deploying the five sample programs takes about a minute.
    - Add `--json` for machine-readable output: one object per program under `{"deploys": [...]}`, or a single object with `--program-path … --json`.

    > **Info**
    >
    > `deploy` confirms submission, not inclusion. Redeploying a program that is already on the sequencer still reports `submitted`, while the sequencer skips the transaction and logs `ProgramAlreadyExists`, which you can see with `logos-scaffold localnet logs`.

1. To deploy a specific program by name:

    ```bash
    RISC0_DEV_MODE=1 logos-scaffold deploy hello_world
    ```

## Step 8: Interact with your program

Use the project-local wallet CLI to submit transactions to your deployed program. The wallet is available at `logos-scaffold wallet`.

1. With the sequencer from Step 6 running, top up the default wallet on your local network, then list your accounts (`wallet list` shows accounts, not a balance):

    ```bash
    logos-scaffold wallet topup
    logos-scaffold wallet list
    ```

    `topup` initialises the account first if it is new, then claims from the Piñata faucet. To confirm the wallet can reach the sequencer, run `logos-scaffold wallet -- check-health`. Everything after `--` goes to the project's wallet binary unchanged.

1. Create a fresh public account for the program to claim. `hello_world` only writes to an account that is uninitialised or already owned by the program, so the topped-up default account does not work:

    ```bash
    logos-scaffold wallet -- account new public
    ```

    The output includes `account_id Public/<ID>`. Pass the part after `Public/` to the runner.

1. Run one of the example runner scripts that submit transactions to your program:

    ```bash
    export NSSA_WALLET_HOME_DIR="$(pwd)/.scaffold/wallet"
    export LEE_WALLET_HOME_DIR="$(pwd)/.scaffold/wallet"
    RISC0_DEV_MODE=1 cargo run --bin run_hello_world -- <ID>
    ```

    The LEZ `v0.1.2` wallet that scaffold pins by default reads `NSSA_WALLET_HOME_DIR`, and LEZ v0.2.0 and later read `LEE_WALLET_HOME_DIR`. Exporting both keeps the runner working on either pin.

    The runner prints the transaction hash. Once the next block is produced, the account holds the greeting `Hola mundo!`, hex-encoded in `data`:

    ```bash
    logos-scaffold wallet -- account get --account-id Public/<ID>
    ```

    ```json
    {"balance":0,"program_owner":"...","data":"486f6c61206d756e646f21","nonce":1}
    ```

    The runner scripts in `src/bin/` demonstrate how to construct and sign a `PublicTransaction`, set the `program_id`, encode an instruction, and submit the transaction via the sequencer RPC.

## Use `logos-scaffold run` for the inner loop

Steps 5 to 8 are often repeated when working on developing an LEZ program. `logos-scaffold run` chains them into one command, and works with no configuration:

```bash
RISC0_DEV_MODE=1 logos-scaffold run
```

It runs these steps in order, printing progress for each:

1. **Build**, which chains `setup` internally.
1. **Build the IDL**, a no-op for projects that are not built on the `lez-framework` template.
1. **Start localnet**, or reuse the one already running.
1. **Top up** the default wallet.
1. **Deploy**, skipped when the guest binaries, IDL, config, and sequencer are all unchanged since the last `run`. A manual `logos-scaffold deploy` does not count, so the first `run` deploys again.
1. **Run `post_deploy` hooks**, if the project configures any.

Useful flags:

| Flag | Effect |
|:---|:---|
| `--profile NAME` | Select a named pipeline from `[run.profiles.<name>]`. |
| `--reset` / `--no-reset` | Wipe sequencer state and wallet and re-seed before the run, or override a config-set default. |
| `--post-deploy <cmd>` | Replace the configured hooks for this run. Repeatable. |
| `--no-post-deploy` | Skip hooks entirely. |
| `--watch` | Re-run the pipeline when files change. |

Configure the loop in `scaffold.toml`:

```toml
[run]
post_deploy = ["cargo run --bin run_hello_world -- <ID>"]

[run.profiles.demo]
topup = false
deploy = false
post_deploy = ["scripts/demo.sh"]
```

- `topup = false` suits a project that funds its own accounts, and `deploy = false` one that deploys from a hook. Both default to `true`.

> **Warning**
>
> A named profile is used as-is: selecting one shadows the inline `[run]` values instead of inheriting them. A key the profile does not state falls back to its own default, not to your `[run]` value. Set every key you need in each profile.

Hooks run through `sh -c` from the project root with these variables set:

| Variable | Value |
|:---|:---|
| `SEQUENCER_URL` | The localnet RPC URL. |
| `NSSA_WALLET_HOME_DIR`, `LEE_WALLET_HOME_DIR` | The project wallet directory, under both the name LEZ `v0.1.2` reads and the one v0.2.0 and later read. |
| `SCAFFOLD_PROJECT_ROOT`, `SCAFFOLD_IDL_DIR` | Absolute paths to the project root and the IDL output directory. |
| `SCAFFOLD_TOPUP_SKIPPED`, `SCAFFOLD_DEPLOY_SKIPPED` | `1` or `0`. Always set, so branch on the value rather than on whether the variable exists. |
| `SCAFFOLD_PROGRAMS` | Space-separated names of the project's deployable programs. |
| `SCAFFOLD_PROGRAM_ID`, `SCAFFOLD_GUEST_BIN` | The deployed program's image ID and guest binary. Set only when the project has exactly one deployable program, so a multi-program project fails loudly instead of picking the wrong one. |

`run` covers the deploy loop only. It does not run any `basecamp` command; for that side of scaffold see [Develop a Logos module with Logos Scaffold](https://docs.logos.co/build-an-app/scaffold/get-started/develop-a-logos-module-with-logos-scaffold.md).

## Deploy to the testnet

> **Warning**
>
> `logos-scaffold` cannot deploy to the current LEZ public testnet. Use the local sequencer from this guide.

The public testnet runs LEZ v0.3, and scaffold pins `v0.1.2` by default. Pointing the project wallet at `https://testnet.lez.logos.co/` fails the compatibility check: `logos-scaffold wallet -- check-health` panics with `Missing authenticated transfer ID from remote`, and `logos-scaffold doctor` reports `FAIL | wallet usability`.

To deploy to the testnet today, set up a standalone wallet as described in [Run an LEZ wallet via the CLI](https://docs.logos.co/lez/get-started/run-lez-wallet-via-cli.md), built from the LEZ release the testnet runs, and use its `deploy-program` command with a guest program built against that same release. Check the wallet with `wallet check-health` first: at the time of writing, a wallet built from LEZ `v0.3.1` passes against the testnet and one built from scaffold's `v0.1.2` pin does not.

## Related documentation

- [About Logos Scaffold](https://docs.logos.co/build-an-app/scaffold/about-logos-scaffold.md)
- [Develop a Logos module with Logos Scaffold](https://docs.logos.co/build-an-app/scaffold/get-started/develop-a-logos-module-with-logos-scaffold.md)
- [Troubleshoot Logos module development with Basecamp](https://docs.logos.co/build-an-app/scaffold/troubleshooting/troubleshoot-logos-module-development-with-basecamp.md)
- [Run the LEZ wallet via CLI](https://docs.logos.co/lez/get-started/run-lez-wallet-via-cli.md)
- [Scaffold command reference](https://github.com/logos-co/scaffold/blob/master/docs/commands.md) and [`scaffold.toml` run configuration](https://github.com/logos-co/scaffold/blob/master/docs/configuration.md) in the scaffold repository

> Source: https://docs.logos.co/lez/rln/register-rln-membership-from-basecamp
> Markdown index of all Logos docs: https://docs.logos.co/llms.txt

# Register an RLN membership from Basecamp

#### Get an RLN membership on the LEZ testnet for a delivery node running in Logos Basecamp.

> **Tip: Version**
>
> This document is accurate for **Testnet v0.3.1**.

This procedure covers how to get an RLN membership on the [LEZ](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#lez) testnet registry for a Logos Delivery node that runs in Logos Basecamp. On the `logos.test` network, a node needs an active membership before any message it sends goes out. You create the node from the Delivery Demo [app](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#app), fund the payer account that the node derives, and the node registers its membership by itself. Use this procedure before you send messages on `logos.test` from Basecamp, for example with the Logos Chat app.

Registration pays with native tokens from the payer account. There is no faucet: you fund the payer yourself, for example by bridging tokens from the Logos Blockchain.

> **Info: Prerequisites**
>
>
> - [Logos Basecamp installed](https://docs.logos.co/basecamp/install-logos-basecamp.md), version [0.3.2](https://github.com/logos-co/logos-basecamp/releases/tag/0.3.2) or later.
> - Network access to the testnet sequencer [`https://testnet.lez.logos.co/`](https://testnet.lez.logos.co/).
> - A way to send `250000000` native units to an account on the LEZ testnet, such as Logos Blockchain notes that you can [bridge to the zone](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/zone-sdk/bridge-assets-between-blockchain-and-zone.md).
> - Approximately 1 GB free disk for the downloaded module packages.

## What to expect

- You can create a `logos.test` delivery node in Basecamp and find the payer account it registers from.
- You can fund the payer and watch the node register its own membership, with no wizard and no faucet.
- You can confirm the membership's state and message quota in the **RLN** panel of Delivery Demo.

## Step 1: Install the Delivery Demo app

1. In Basecamp's **Package Manager**, find **Delivery Demo** in the official catalogue and click **INSTALL**.
1. In the **Install Package?** dialogue, click **Install**.

   - The dialogue lists `delivery_module` 0.4.0, `liblogos_lez_rln_module` 5.1.0, and `liblogos_rln_module` 0.12.0. These modules hold the node's wallet and register its membership. No extra package repository is needed.

   **Expected result:** the **Delivery Demo** row reads **INSTALLED**. If the row shows **RETRY**, click it once more.

## Step 2: Create the delivery node

1. Open **Delivery Demo** from the **Applications** grid.
1. In the `createNode` panel, keep `preset` set to `logos.test` and `mode` set to `Core`, then click **Call**.

   **Expected result:** the status badges read `RLN READY` and `CONNECTED`. The **RLN** panel shows **Membership** `unknown` and **Messages left this epoch** `0 / 0`, because the node has no membership yet.

   ![Delivery Demo after creating the node, with the RLN panel showing Membership unknown and 0 / 0 messages left](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/logos-co/logos-docs/main/docs/lez/assets/register-rln-membership-from-basecamp/delivery-demo-membership-unknown.png)

## Step 3: Find the payer account

Creating the node also creates its LEZ wallet and derives a payer account from it. The payer pays for the registration.

1. Read the payer account ID from the wallet in Basecamp's data directory. On Linux, with the default data directory:

   ```bash
   cat ~/.local/share/Logos/LogosBasecamp/module_data/liblogos_lez_rln_module/*/wallet-home/payer.json
   ```

   **Expected result:** a 64-character hex account ID.

   - If you started Basecamp with `--user-dir <path>`, replace `~/.local/share/Logos/LogosBasecamp` with that path.
   - Basecamp's log also names the payer, in a line that reads `derived the payer <ACCOUNT> — it holds nothing until something transfers to it`.

1. Convert the account ID to the base58 form that the sequencer and LEZ wallets use. Replace `<ACCOUNT>` with the hex value:

   ```bash
   ACCOUNT=<ACCOUNT>
   python3 -c '
   import sys
   A = "123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz"
   h = sys.argv[1]
   n, s = int(h, 16), ""
   while n:
       n, r = divmod(n, 58)
       s = A[r] + s
   print("1" * ((len(h) - len(h.lstrip("0"))) // 2) + s)' $ACCOUNT
   ```

## Step 4: Fund the payer account

To register, the payer must hold the registry's price plus a fee reserve: `182800000` native units in total at the testnet's minimum fee. Sending `250000000` leaves headroom. A registration spends about `75000000`, and the rest stays in the payer account.

1. Send `250000000` native units to the payer account.

   - To bridge from the Logos Blockchain, follow [Bridge assets between Logos Blockchain and a Zone](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/zone-sdk/bridge-assets-between-blockchain-and-zone.md), with the payer account ID as the deposit's recipient. A deposit is credited on LEZ only once it is final on the blockchain, which takes about 10 hours on the current testnet.

1. Check the payer's balance. Replace `<BASE58>` with the value from Step 3:

   ```bash
   curl -sS -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"getAccountBalance","params":["<BASE58>"],"id":1}' \
     https://testnet.lez.logos.co/
   ```

   **Expected result:** `result` is at or above `182800000`.

## Step 5: Wait for the membership to register

The node registers its membership as soon as it sees a funded payer.

1. Keep Basecamp running with the node from Step 2.

   - If you closed Basecamp after Step 2, start it again, open **Delivery Demo**, and click **Call** in the `createNode` panel with the same values. The node finds the funded payer and registers.

1. Watch the **RLN** panel in Delivery Demo.

   **Expected result:** within a few minutes of the payer being funded, **Membership** reads `active`, **Messages left this epoch** reads `100 / 100`, and a **Membership** hash appears below.

   ![The RLN panel of Delivery Demo showing Membership active, 100 / 100 messages left, and the membership hash](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/logos-co/logos-docs/main/docs/lez/assets/register-rln-membership-from-basecamp/delivery-demo-membership-active.png)

The membership is stored with the node's wallet in Basecamp's data directory. Later launches of Basecamp pick it up, and nothing is registered or paid again.

## Troubleshooting RLN membership in Basecamp

### The RLN Membership app shows "Setup failed" with `bridge_failure: Call refused`

The **RLN Membership** app (`rln_membership_ui` 0.7.4) from the **Logos RLN Membership** package repository registers through a faucet that the current RLN modules no longer have. It can't complete on the current testnet. Register through a delivery node as described on this page instead. You can remove the **Logos RLN Membership** repository under **Manage Repositories**.

### Membership stays `unknown`

The payer holds less than `182800000`. Check its balance as in [Step 4](#step-4-fund-the-payer-account). A bridge deposit shows up on LEZ only about 10 hours after it is included on the blockchain.

### The balance check returns `0` long after a bridge deposit

The deposit isn't final on the blockchain yet. Wait, and check that the deposit's recipient was the payer account ID from [Step 3](#step-3-find-the-payer-account).

---

> Source: https://docs.logos.co/lez/rln/register-rln-membership-on-lez-with-delivery-node
> Markdown index of all Logos docs: https://docs.logos.co/llms.txt

# Register an RLN membership on LEZ with a Delivery node

#### Start a Logos Delivery node on the DoS-protected logos.test network, register its RLN membership on the Logos Execution Zone, and send a rate-limited message.

> **Tip: Version**
>
> This document is accurate for **Testnet v0.3.0**.

This procedure shows how to register an Rate-Limiting Nullifier (RLN) membership on the [Logos Execution Zone](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#logos-execution-zone), used to protect against denial-of-service attacks. Messages published on the LEZ must include a proof of membership. It is intended for node operators who want to join the DoS-protected network, and touches Logos Core, [Logos Delivery](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#logos-delivery), and LEZ in a single flow.

> **Info: Prerequisites**
>
>
> - A supported OS:
>    - macOS (Apple Silicon)
>    - Linux (x86-64 or aarch64)
> - [`logosctl`](https://github.com/logos-co/logos-logoscore-cli/releases/tag/0.3.2) installed.
>    - Install it by running `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/logos-co/logos-docs/main/resources/scripts/install-logosctl.sh | sudo sh`
> - `curl` and `python3`
> - Network access to `github.com` for the catalogue downloads, and to the testnet sequencer at `https://testnet.lez.logos.co/`
> - About 1 GB of free disk space. The [modules](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#module) take about 300 MB.
> - `250000000` units of native LEZ tokens for the node's payer [account](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#account), from one of these sources:
>    - A [Logos Blockchain](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#logos-blockchain) wallet you can [bridge assets](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/transfer-tokens/bridge-assets-from-logos-blockchain-to-zone-on-basecamp.md) from. Testnet has no faucet.
>    - A LEZ account you already hold on the testnet zone, with about `270000000` units so it can cover the transfer's fee reserve.
>

## What to expect

- You can run a `delivery_module` node on `logos.test` with an active RLN membership registered on LEZ.
- You can fund the node's payer account and watch the node register its membership by itself.
- You can send a message that carries an RLN proof and confirm that it propagated and used up part of your epoch quota.

## Step 1: Set up a working directory

Run every command in this procedure in one shell, from one working directory.

1. Create a working directory and change into it:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/logos-rln && cd ~/logos-rln
   ```

1. Set the session directory. Every `logosctl` command in this shell uses it to hold the daemon's state, its logs, and the installed modules:

   ```bash
   export LOGOSCTL_CONFIG_DIR=$PWD/session
   ```

## Step 2: Start the daemon with a wallet home

The node keeps its wallet, including its private key, in a wallet home directory. There is nothing to configure: the `logos.test` preset names the registry as `logos:testnet:<config account>`, and the LEZ RLN module maps `testnet` to the testnet sequencer from its built-in network table. The directory only fixes where the wallet lives.

1. Create an empty wallet home:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p wallet-home
   ```

1. Start the daemon. It passes its environment to the modules, which is how the wallet finds its home:

   ```bash
   LEE_WALLET_HOME_DIR=$PWD/wallet-home \
   NSSA_WALLET_HOME_DIR=$PWD/wallet-home \
     logosctl daemon start --detach
   ```

   **Expected result:** `Daemon started (pid N)` and the path of its log, `session/logs/daemon.log`. The command returns once the daemon is ready.

1. Check the daemon's status:

   ```bash
   logosctl daemon status --json
   ```

   **Expected result:** `"daemon":{"status":"running",...}`, with `capability_module`, `package_manager`, and `package_downloader` loaded.

## Step 3: Install and load the modules

1. Install the [delivery module](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#delivery-module) and the RLN module from the official [catalogue](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#catalogue). `liblogos_rln_module` pulls in `liblogos_lez_rln_module`:

   ```bash
   logosctl package install delivery_module liblogos_rln_module -y
   ```

1. List the installed [packages](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#package):

   ```bash
   logosctl package ls
   ```

   **Expected result:** `delivery_module` 0.3.3 or later, `liblogos_rln_module` 0.12.0 or later, and `liblogos_lez_rln_module` 5.1.0 or later, each with source `user`.

   - Older delivery modules point `logos.test` at a registry that is no longer used, and older LEZ RLN modules link a LEZ wallet that can't sync the LEZ v0.3.1 testnet zone.

1. Load the delivery module. This also loads the RLN modules, which are its optional dependencies:

   ```bash
   logosctl module load delivery_module
   logosctl module ls --loaded
   ```

   **Expected result:** `liblogos_lez_rln_module`, `liblogos_rln_module`, and `delivery_module` are loaded.

## Step 4: Create the delivery node

1. Capture the node's events in the background. The watcher only sees events emitted after it attaches, so start it first:

   ```bash
   logosctl --json watch delivery_module >> events.jsonl 2>&1 &
   ```

1. Write the node config and create the node:

   ```bash
   cat > node.json <<'EOF'
   {"mode": "Core", "preset": "logos.test"}
   EOF
   logosctl --json call delivery_module createNode @$PWD/node.json
   ```

   | Field | Purpose |
   |:------|:--------|
   | `mode` | `Core` runs a full relay node. |
   | `preset` | `logos.test` brings the network settings (cluster 2, 8 auto-shards, built-in entry nodes) and its RLN settings: the registry on the LEZ testnet, the RLN identifier, and the epoch size. |
   | `messagingOverrides` | Optional per-layer settings, for example `{"tcp-port": 30303}`. Keep extra keys inside it: a bare top-level key switches parsing to the legacy flat shape. |

   **Expected result:** `"success":true`. Creating the node also starts the RLN module on the registry that the preset names. The LEZ RLN module writes `wallet-home/wallet_config.json`, pointing at the testnet sequencer, and `wallet-home/network.json`, containing `{"network":"testnet","source":"table"}`. From here on, the node registers itself once its payer account is funded.

1. Poll the RLN state until it reports `"state":"Ready"`:

   ```bash
   logosctl --json call delivery_module rlnState
   ```

   **Expected result:** the reply names the RLN scope the node uses:

   ```text
   "registryId":"logos:testnet:<64 hex>", "rlnIdentifier":"<64 hex>", "epochSizeSec":<N>
   ```

1. Keep both values for the RLN calls in later steps. Replace `<registryId>` and `<rlnIdentifier>` with the values from the reply. Write the identifier to a file so that `logosctl` can't mistake it for a number:

   ```bash
   REGISTRY=<registryId>
   printf '%s' '<rlnIdentifier>' > rln-id.arg
   ```

## Step 5: Fund the node's payer account

The node derives a payer account from its wallet. To register, it must hold the registry's price plus a fee reserve derived from the chain's base fee: `182800000` in total at the testnet's minimum fee, and more if fees rise. Sending `250000000` native units leaves headroom. The unused part of the reserve is refunded: a registration spends about `75000000`, and the rest stays in the payer account.

1. Poll the wallet status until `state` is `ready`:

   ```bash
   logosctl --json call liblogos_lez_rln_module wallet_status
   ```

   **Expected result:** `{"status":"ok","result":{... "state":"ready", "network":"testnet", "payer":"<ACCOUNT>" ...}}`. While the wallet syncs, `state` is `pending`.

1. Convert the payer account ID to the `Public/<base58>` form that LEZ wallets and explorers use. Replace `<ACCOUNT>` with the 64-character hex value of `payer`, which is also the recipient a bridge deposit carries:

   ```bash
   ACCOUNT=<ACCOUNT>
   python3 -c '
   import sys
   A = "123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz"
   h = sys.argv[1]
   n, s = int(h, 16), ""
   while n:
       n, r = divmod(n, 58)
       s = A[r] + s
   print("Public/" + "1" * ((len(h) - len(h.lstrip("0"))) // 2) + s)' $ACCOUNT
   ```

1. Send `250000000` native units to the payer account:

   - To bridge from the Logos Blockchain, follow [Bridge assets between the blockchain and a zone](https://docs.logos.co/blockchain/zone-sdk/bridge-assets-between-blockchain-and-zone.md). A deposit is credited on LEZ only once it is final on the blockchain. On the current testnet that is about 10 hours after the deposit is included in a block, and the payer balance stays unchanged until then. The deposit's fee is paid on the blockchain side.
   - To transfer from an existing LEZ account, send to the `Public/<base58>` address. A transfer carries a fee reserve of about `19000000` on top of the amount, at the minimum fee for the wallet's standard 2M gas limit; all but the actual fee (about `100000`) is refunded to the sender.

1. Check the payer's balance. An empty argument file means the node's own payer:

   ```bash
   : > self.arg
   logosctl --json call liblogos_lez_rln_module get_native_balance @$PWD/self.arg
   ```

   **Expected result:** `balance` is at or above the amount you sent.

## Step 6: Wait for the membership to register

The node registers itself on the LEZ registry, typically one to three minutes after the funding lands.

1. Poll the membership state until `state` is `active`:

   ```bash
   logosctl --json call liblogos_rln_module get_membership_state $REGISTRY @$PWD/rln-id.arg
   ```

   - While registering, the reply shows `"state":"unknown"` and `"provisioning":{"step":"awaiting_funding"}` or `"step":"registering"`.
   - Once the registration is submitted, the reply shows `"state":"pending"` with a `leaf_index`, until the transaction is in a LEZ block.

   **Expected result:** `"state":"active"` (or `"grace_period"`), with a `leaf_index` and a `membership_hash`. `"state":"failed"` means registration failed; see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting-rln-membership). If `daemon.log` says `no membership within 300s`, the module only stopped waiting: check that the sequencer is producing blocks with `getLastBlockId`, and keep polling.

## Step 7: Start the node and send a message

The node only starts with an active membership.

1. Start the node and check that it reported `nodeStarted`:

   ```bash
   logosctl --json call delivery_module start
   until grep nodeStarted events.jsonl; do sleep 1; done
   ```

1. Wait about 15 seconds for the node to join the [Relay](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#relay) mesh, then subscribe to a [content topic](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#content-topic):

   ```bash
   sleep 15
   TOPIC=/my-app/1/hello/proto
   logosctl --json call delivery_module subscribe $TOPIC
   ```

1. Note the epoch quota before sending. The `str:` prefix passes the timestamp as a string:

   ```bash
   logosctl --json call liblogos_rln_module get_epoch_quota $REGISTRY @$PWD/rln-id.arg str:$(date +%s)
   ```

   **Expected result:** `{"epoch_index":N,"rate_limit":N,"remaining":N}`.

1. Send a message:

   ```bash
   printf '%s' "hello from my node" > payload.arg
   logosctl --json call delivery_module send $TOPIC @$PWD/payload.arg
   ```

   **Expected result:** `"success":true`, with a `requestId` as the value.

1. Check that the node generated a proof and the message propagated:

   ```bash
   grep -iE 'rlnGenerateProofRequest|messagePropagated|messageError' events.jsonl
   ```

   **Expected result:** within about 30 seconds, a proof-generation request for the send (`rlnGenerateProofRequest` or `dispatchRlnGenerateProofRequestEvent`), then:

   ```text
   {"event":"messagePropagated","data":{"arg0":"<requestId>","arg1":"<message hash>"}}
   ```

   - A `messageError` event with your `requestId` means the send failed; its data carries the reason.

1. Run the `get_epoch_quota` call again.

   **Expected result:** in the same `epoch_index`, `remaining` is lower than before the send.

1. Stop the daemon when you're finished:

   ```bash
   logosctl daemon stop
   ```

   - The wallet, membership, and installed packages stay in `wallet-home/` and `session/`. To run the node again, start the daemon with the same environment as in [Step 2](#step-2-start-the-daemon-with-a-wallet-home), then `module load delivery_module`, start the event watcher, run `createNode` with the same `node.json`, and `start` once `rlnState` is `Ready`. The existing membership is picked up; nothing is registered or paid again.

## Troubleshooting RLN membership

### A string argument arrives as a number

`logosctl call` converts arguments that look numeric, which can catch a hex RLN identifier, a hash, or a payload. Write the value to a file with no trailing newline (`printf '%s'`) and pass it as `@/absolute/path`; the file's contents are passed verbatim as a string. A `str:<value>` prefix also forces a string.

### `createNode` fails with an unknown preset

Spell the preset exactly `logos.test`. `logostest` is rejected, not treated as an alias.

### `rlnState` stays `Disabled`

The installed `delivery_module` is older than 0.3.0, where `logos.test` has RLN turned off. Check the version with `logosctl package ls` and upgrade with `logosctl package install delivery_module -y`.

### `rlnState` reports `Failed`

The reply carries the reason. A common one is a hand-written `wallet_config.json`, or a `LEZ_RLN_SEQUENCER` variable, pointing at a sequencer that isn't the testnet one, so the registry can't be found on-chain. Start with an empty `wallet-home/` to let the module pick the sequencer. The module reads `LEZ_RLN_SEQUENCER` only when `wallet-home/` has no `wallet_config.json` yet, and never rewrites an existing one.

Another is a `delivery_module` older than 0.3.3, whose `logos.test` preset names the old registry `logos:testnet:841312e9…`, which is no longer used. Check the version with `logosctl package ls`, and upgrade with `logosctl package install delivery_module -y`.

### `wallet_status` reports `failed`, or `daemon.log` shows `Unexpected variant tag`

The installed `liblogos_lez_rln_module` is older than 5.1.0 and links a LEZ v0.3.0 wallet, which can't read LEZ v0.3.1 blocks. The log line reads `Sync failed: Parse error: Unexpected variant tag`. Run `logosctl catalog refresh`, upgrade with `logosctl package install liblogos_lez_rln_module -y`, and start again with a fresh `wallet-home/`.

### `wallet_status` stays `pending` with the network selected

The node can't reach the testnet sequencer. Check it from the same machine, using the `sequencer_addr` from `wallet-home/wallet_config.json` (`https://testnet.lez.logos.co/` with current modules); this request should answer with a block number:

```bash
curl -sS -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"getLastBlockId","params":[],"id":1}' \
  https://testnet.lez.logos.co/
```

### `wallet_status` stays `pending` with `no network selected`

Nothing has named a registry yet. Run `createNode` with the `logos.test` preset as in [Step 4](#step-4-create-the-delivery-node). If it persists, the installed RLN modules are too old; see [Step 3](#step-3-install-and-load-the-modules).

### The wallet never becomes ready, or opens in the wrong place

The wallet home variables were not set on the `daemon start` command; the modules only see the daemon's environment. Stop the daemon and start it again with them.

### Registry calls fail with `bound to network`

`wallet-home/` was used for another network before. A wallet home bound to one network refuses another. Use a fresh wallet home per network.

### `provisioning.step` stays at `awaiting_funding`

The node waits indefinitely for its payer balance. Check `get_native_balance` and complete the funding transfer.

### Registration fails with `Incorrect fee`

The payer holds less than the price plus the fee reserve (`182800000` in total at the minimum fee). Top it up to `250000000`.

### Registration never finishes and `daemon.log` contains `outside registry bounds`

The registry rejected the requested rate limit. The log line names the allowed range.

### `get_epoch_quota` returns `rate_limit: 0`

The node has no usable membership yet; the quota is not exhausted. Wait for `get_membership_state` to report `active`.

### `send` fails with `no_usable_membership`

Registration has not finished. Wait for `get_membership_state` to report `active`.

### Receivers drop the first message after registration

A newly published tree root takes up to one root window to reach other nodes. Later sends are unaffected.

### `daemon start` fails, or `daemon status` reports `not_running`

Read `session/daemon/startup.err` and `session/logs/daemon.log`.

### Every command fails with `no daemon`

The command isn't using the daemon's session. Check that `LOGOSCTL_CONFIG_DIR` and `TMPDIR` match the ones the daemon was started with; the daemon's local socket lives in `TMPDIR`. Don't run the daemon under a private `/tmp`, such as systemd's `PrivateTmp=yes`.

### `package install` does nothing and asks for confirmation

Without a terminal, `package install` refuses to proceed unless given `-y`.

### `package install` can't find `liblogos_rln_module`

The session's catalogue index is stale. Run `logosctl catalog refresh`. `logosctl catalog ls` lists the enabled catalogues; the official one, `logos-modules-official`, must be enabled.

### After a restart the membership reads `unknown` and sends fail

A module process from the previous daemon outlived `daemon stop` and still holds the node's ports and the RLN keystore. Stop the daemon, look for processes left over from the previous daemon with `ps -ef | grep logos`, end them, and start again.

---

> Source: https://docs.logos.co/lez/extensions/admin-authority
> Markdown index of all Logos docs: https://docs.logos.co/llms.txt

# Gate program instructions with admin-authority

> **Warning**
>
> This page is an early draft and may be incomplete or incorrect. Expect changes, missing prerequisites, and commands that might not work in your setup. This content is still being completed and verified.
>
> The dependency snippets pin `admin-authority` v0.2.0 and the framework at the upstream `v0.7.0` tag, the first release that carries the extension mechanism ([logos-co/spel#257](https://github.com/logos-co/spel/pull/257)).

`admin-authority` is a SPEL extension that adds a single transferable admin role to your [LEZ](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#lez) program. The admin is the only [account](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#account) allowed to call admin-gated instructions. The role can be transferred to another signer or [PDA](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#pda), or renounced permanently. This page walks through using `admin-authority` from an app developer's perspective. If you are building a different extension, see [Build a SPEL extension library](https://docs.logos.co/lez/extensions/build-a-spel-extension-library.md) instead.

## When to use it

Pick `admin-authority` when your [program](https://docs.logos.co/get-started/glossary.md#program) has:

- A configuration or policy account that only one party should mutate (`set_fee_bps`, `update_oracle_address`, `pause`).
- An emergency action that needs guarded access (`recover_funds`, `migrate_state`).
- A handoff scenario where ownership might rotate between parties over time.

If your program needs multi-party approval rather than single-admin gating, `admin-authority` is the wrong primitive, wait for `multisig-authority` (RFP-TBD) or compose admin-authority with a multisig PDA as the admin.

## Prerequisites

You need a stable Rust toolchain, git, and the native build tools the dependency tree leans on. The `spel` CLI additionally needs `unzip` (the `rust-rapidsnark` build script downloads a prebuilt zip and unpacks it through a helper shell script), the Python development library (a transitive dependency links against libpython through `pyo3`), and the PC/SC smart card library (the wallet crate it builds links `pcsc`). The verification step at the end uses `jq`. On a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 this covers everything:

```bash
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y curl git build-essential pkg-config libssl-dev ca-certificates unzip python3 python3-dev cmake libpcsclite-dev jq
```

Two different floors apply here, and neither comes from `admin-authority` itself, which declares only `rust-version = "1.88"`. Building your program needs rustc 1.90 or newer whenever `ruint` resolves freely, the floor its 1.20.0 release sets. A `spel init` scaffold pins `ruint = "=1.17.0"` in its guest manifest, so that particular floor does not apply on the scaffold route. Installing the `spel` CLI needs rustc 1.94.0 or newer: a transitive `logos-blockchain` crate uses `strict_overflow_ops`, which older toolchains reject as an unstable feature. The CLI pins `channel = "1.94.0"` in its own `rust-toolchain.toml`, but `cargo install --git` does not apply a dependency's toolchain file, so your default toolchain has to meet that floor itself. Verified in a clean Ubuntu 24.04 container on rustc 1.99.0: the CLI installs from the tag, the scaffolded program builds and deploys, and every command on this page ran against a local LEZ v0.2.4 sequencer, both handovers included. The deploy and the lifecycle commands, both handovers and renounce included, also ran on the public legacy testnet.

## Add the dependency

In your program's `Cargo.toml`. If you do not have a program crate yet, do [Install the `spel` CLI](#install-the-spel-cli) and the `spel init` command in [Annotate the module](#annotate-the-module) first, then come back here. For a `spel init` scaffold the manifest to edit is `methods/guest/Cargo.toml`, not the root manifest, which is a `[workspace]` excluding `methods/guest`. That guest manifest already carries its own `[dependencies]` table, holding `spel-framework`, `nssa_core`, `risc0-zkvm`, your project's `_core` crate, `serde`, `borsh` and the `ruint = "=1.17.0"` pin from the prerequisites, so merge the entries below into it rather than appending a second table, which cargo rejects outright with `error: duplicate key`. Scaffolded with the source flags from [Annotate the module](#annotate-the-module), its `spel-framework` and `nssa_core` pins already match these, so `admin-authority` is the only line you add:

```toml
[dependencies]
admin-authority = { git = "https://github.com/mmlado/spel-admin-authority", tag = "v0.2.0" }
spel-framework  = { git = "https://github.com/logos-co/spel", tag = "v0.7.0" }
nssa_core = { git = "https://github.com/logos-blockchain/logos-execution-zone.git", tag = "v0.2.4", package = "lee_core" }
borsh = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
```

All five are needed: the reference samples use exactly this set. `nssa_core` carries the on-chain account types, `borsh` encodes your state, and `serde` is required by the instruction plumbing even when your own types never touch it. The `admin-authority-macros` sub-crate is pulled in transitively. You do not need to declare it directly.

The `spel-framework` entry must be the reference `admin-authority` itself pins, the `v0.7.0` tag, spelt the same way. The library README names it for each release. Cargo identifies a git dependency by its reference, so a branch, another tag, or even a `rev` pointing at the same commit puts two copies of the framework into your dependency graph, and the build fails with a `From<AdminError>` trait error plus name resolution errors inside the `require_admin` expansion.

After adding the dependencies, run `cargo fetch` once from `methods/guest`, not from the project root. The scaffold's root `Cargo.toml` excludes `methods/guest`, so a root `cargo fetch` resolves a graph that does not contain `admin-authority`: it still updates the workspace's own registry and git sources and exits 0, so nothing in its output tells you the extension was skipped. The framework's extension scanner resolves your dependency graph with an offline metadata call, which fails deterministically for a fresh consumer whose git dependencies were never fetched.

## Install the `spel` CLI

The lifecycle commands below and the IDL check at the end use the `spel` CLI. Install it from the same upstream tag the framework dependency pins:

```bash
cargo install --git https://github.com/logos-co/spel --tag v0.7.0 spel
```

The package name is `spel`, not `spel-cli` as the repository directory suggests, asking cargo for `spel-cli` fails with "could not find `spel-cli`."

This build also reaches the network beyond fetching crates: a transitive build script downloads a prebuilt `logos-blockchain-circuits` artifact from GitHub releases. It does not honour the usual CA environment variables, so behind a TLS-inspecting proxy it fails with `invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer` partway through the build. If the download cannot reach GitHub directly, either point `LBC_ROOT_DIR` at a local circuits build, or pre-seed the cache using a tool that does honour your CA bundle:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.cache/logos/blockchain
curl -fL https://github.com/logos-blockchain/logos-blockchain-circuits/releases/download/v0.5.3/logos-blockchain-circuits-v0.5.3-linux-x86_64.tar.gz \
  | tar xz -C ~/.cache/logos/blockchain/
```

The version has to match the `logos-blockchain-circuits` version the pinned framework resolves to, `v0.5.3` for `v0.7.0`. The build script reuses any artifact directory it finds there and skips the download entirely.

## Annotate the module

This page assumes you already have an LEZ program crate. A deployable one is a RISC Zero guest, and `spel init` scaffolds it at `methods/guest/src/bin/<name>.rs`, where `<name>` is the project name with hyphens replaced by underscores, so `spel init my-program` writes `my_program.rs`. That is the same layout `spel generate-idl` auto-detects when given no path. Pass both source flags ahead of the project name, the parser stops reading flags at the first argument that is not one, so anything after the name is dropped without a warning. With the default pins the scaffold takes `logos-co/spel` at its `main` branch. A branch never unifies with the tag `admin-authority` pins, and as it moves its `lee_core` can differ too. Either way the guest ends up with two copies of the framework and fails to compile with type errors out of the `#[lez_program]` expansion rather than anything naming the marker. Pass the tag:

```bash
spel init \
    --spel-git https://github.com/logos-co/spel.git \
    --spel-tag v0.7.0 \
    my-program
```

If you only want to check the integration and started from `cargo new`, delete the default `fn main` first. The `#[lez_program]` macro generates the program's entry point, and the leftover stub collides with it as a duplicate `main`.

Add `#[admin_authority]` to your `#[lez_program]` module, directly below the `#[lez_program]` attribute:

```rust
use spel_framework::prelude::*;

#[lez_program]
#[admin_authority]
mod my_program {
    #[instruction]
    pub fn create_pool(
        #[account(init, pda = literal("pool_config"))] config: AccountWithMetadata,
    ) -> SpelResult { /* writes the initial PoolConfig */ }
}
```

Nothing is imported from the library at this point. The `#[admin_authority]` marker is consumed by the framework's scanner during expansion, not resolved as an import, so importing the name only earns an unused import warning. The gate attribute gets imported when the first instruction uses it, next section. The module body does not need `use super::*;` either, the macro resolves paths to items declared outside the module on its own.

That single annotation exposes five new instructions in your program's IDL:

| Instruction | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `admin_initialize` | Creates the admin Config PDA and installs the caller as the first admin. Must be called once after deployment. |
| `admin_transfer` | Replaces the current admin with a new signer or PDA in one transaction. |
| `admin_nominate` | Names the next admin. Nothing changes until the nominee accepts. |
| `admin_accept` | The nominee signs alone and becomes admin. |
| `admin_renounce` | Zeros the admin permanently. Terminal, no recovery path. |

> **Warning**
>
> **Initialisation window.** Until `admin_initialize` is called, the admin Config PDA does not exist. Unless you build with a genesis key, see [Fix the first admin at build time](#fix-the-first-admin-at-build-time), anyone who submits the first `admin_initialize` becomes the admin. Send it as the very next transaction after deployment to prevent a third party from claiming the role. Bundling with the deployment itself is not possible today because a LEZ deployment transaction carries no instructions.

## Gate an instruction

Add `#[require_admin]` to any instruction that should only succeed when the caller is the current admin:

```rust
#[account_type]
#[derive(BorshSerialize, BorshDeserialize, Clone, Debug)]
pub struct PoolConfig {
    pub fee_bps: u32,
}

// ... inside the #[lez_program] module:
use admin_authority::require_admin;

#[instruction]
#[require_admin]
pub fn set_fee_bps(
    #[account(mut, pda = literal("pool_config"))] mut config: AccountWithMetadata,
    new_fee_bps: u32,
) -> SpelResult {
    // The admin check has already run.
    PoolConfig { fee_bps: new_fee_bps }.write_to(&mut config)?;
    Ok(SpelOutput::execute(vec![config], vec![]))
}
```

The `write_to` helper is yours to write, the library does not provide it. The reference sample uses this one:

```rust
impl PoolConfig {
    fn write_to(&self, account: &mut AccountWithMetadata) -> Result<(), SpelError> {
        account.account.data = borsh::to_vec(self)
            .map_err(|_| SpelError::SerializationError { message: "encoding failed".into() })?
            .try_into()
            .map_err(|_| SpelError::SerializationError { message: "data too large".into() })?;
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

Keep the arguments of instructions you call from the `spel` CLI to the types `spel --help` lists, such as `u8`, `u32`, `u64` and byte arrays. It has no encoding for `u16` and refuses such a call before sending it.

The `#[account_type]` struct sits outside the `#[lez_program]` module, the instruction inside it. The handler returns `Ok(SpelOutput::execute(post_states, messages))`, where `post_states` lists your declared accounts in declaration order. The injected `admin_config` and `caller` are prepended to the post-states automatically, ahead of the accounts you declared, you only handle the parameters you wrote.

The gate needs two accounts, the `admin_config` PDA holding the current admin state and a signing `caller`. You do not have to write them: the framework injects both from metadata the library declares, and they appear in the IDL like declared parameters. Declaring them explicitly produces the same program only if you declare them ahead of your own parameters and in the injected order, `admin_config` then `caller`. They are then your parameters, appearing in your post-states list like any other account. Declaring them after your own parameters still compiles, but it reorders the instruction's accounts in the IDL, and that order is the transaction ABI.

If your instruction already has parameters by different names, point the gate at them with the inject-account names as keys: `#[require_admin(admin_config = my_cfg, caller = owner)]`. Use that form whenever either name differs. The framework does reuse a declared `#[account(signer)]` parameter, or a PDA parameter with the matching seed, in the instruction's account list rather than injecting it twice, but the gate's prologue still refers to the accounts by their role names, so a bare `#[require_admin]` over a renamed parameter fails to compile with `cannot find value caller in this scope` pointed at the attribute.

## Build and deploy the program

The scaffold's `make build` runs `cargo risczero build`, which compiles the guest in Docker. With framework `v0.7.0` that build fails for a program whose extensions are git dependencies: inside Docker the extension scanner cannot resolve the dependency graph offline, and it stops with `marker(s) ["admin_authority"] matched no discoverable extension and dependency resolution failed`. Build natively through the scaffold's `methods` crate instead. That needs the RISC Zero toolchain:

```bash
curl -L https://risczero.com/install | bash
rzup install
```

Tell the `methods` crate which guest to build, in `methods/Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[package.metadata.risc0]
methods = ["guest"]
```

Then build from the project root and read the program id:

```bash
cargo build --release -p my_program-methods
spel program-id target/riscv-guest/my_program-methods/my_program-guest/riscv32im-risc0-zkvm-elf/release/my_program.bin
```

The value under `ImageID (hex bytes)` is the program id every command below takes as `--program`. Deploy the same file with the LEZ `wallet` CLI, installed from the LEZ release your `nssa_core` pin names. The wallet and the `spel` CLI both read their configuration, including the sequencer address, from the directory `LEE_WALLET_HOME_DIR` points at.

The public LEZ legacy testnet runs v0.2.4, the release this page builds against. Point a new wallet home at its sequencer, check the connection, and deploy:

```bash
cargo install --git https://github.com/logos-blockchain/logos-execution-zone.git --tag v0.2.4 wallet
export LEE_WALLET_HOME_DIR=~/lez-wallet
wallet change-network https://testnet-legacy.lez.logos.co
wallet check-health
wallet deploy-program target/riscv-guest/my_program-methods/my_program-guest/riscv32im-risc0-zkvm-elf/release/my_program.bin
```

On a new wallet home, `change-network` first sets up the wallet. It asks for a password and prints a recovery phrase. The [legacy testnet explorer](https://explorer.testnet-legacy.lez.logos.co/) shows the blocks.

Blocks on the legacy testnet are about a minute apart, so a command can report `Transaction NOT confirmed: Transaction not found in preconfigured amount of blocks` from `spel`, or `Error: All pollers failed` from `wallet auth-transfer init`, and still land a block later. `wallet account get --account-id Public/<account-id>` shows the `nonce` of a key, which goes up by one when a transaction it signed lands. Wait for that before you send the next transaction from the same key. A transaction built while the previous one is still pending reuses its nonce and does not land.

To test against a local sequencer instead, build the standalone sequencer from the same LEZ release and start it in its own terminal. It listens on `127.0.0.1:3040` and keeps its state in the directory you start it from:

```bash
git clone --branch v0.2.4 https://github.com/logos-blockchain/logos-execution-zone.git ~/lez
(cd ~/lez && cargo build --release --features standalone -p sequencer_service)
mkdir -p ~/lez-sequencer && cp ~/lez/lez/sequencer/service/configs/debug/sequencer_config.json ~/lez-sequencer/
cd ~/lez-sequencer && RUST_LOG=info ~/lez/target/release/sequencer_service ./sequencer_config.json
```

In another terminal, from the project root, point a wallet home at that sequencer and deploy:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/lez-wallet-local && cp ~/lez/lez/wallet/configs/debug/wallet_config.json ~/lez-wallet-local/
export LEE_WALLET_HOME_DIR=~/lez-wallet-local
wallet check-health
wallet deploy-program target/riscv-guest/my_program-methods/my_program-guest/riscv32im-risc0-zkvm-elf/release/my_program.bin
```

## Become the first admin

`admin_initialize` takes no arguments. The signing caller becomes the admin (self-election). There is no candidate argument at initialise because the LEZ duplicate-account rule rejects a transaction listing the same account twice, so a caller could never also pass itself as candidate evidence.

The admin key must be owned by a program. A key that has never been used is owned by none, and on LEZ v0.2.1 to v0.2.4 such a key can sign once and is then rejected in every later transaction. `admin-authority` therefore refuses it as admin with program error 6112, `admin key is owned by no program`. If your wallet has no public account yet, create one. It prints `Generated new account with account_id Public/<your-account-id>`, and the commands below take the id without the `Public/` prefix. Then claim the key:

```bash
wallet account new public
wallet auth-transfer init --account-id Public/<your-account-id>
```

Every lifecycle command below reads your program's IDL from a file. Generate it once from the program you just built:

```bash
# From a `spel init` project root, drop the path entirely and the guest is auto-detected.
spel generate-idl path/to/your/program/src/main.rs > program-idl.json
```

To check a command without submitting it, add `--dry-run=text` before the `--` separator. It resolves the accounts and arguments and prints the transaction it would send, which is the only way to validate an invocation before you have a node to submit to.

```bash
spel --idl program-idl.json --program <program-id> -- \
    admin-initialize --caller <your-account-id>
```

When the sequencer rejects a transaction, the CLI only reports `Transaction NOT confirmed: Transaction not found in preconfigured amount of blocks`. The reason is in the sequencer log as program error 6000 plus the library's error code, for example `Program error [6103]: ... signer is not the current admin`. The public testnet does not publish its log, so to see the code, run the failing call against a local sequencer. The [library README](https://github.com/mmlado/spel-admin-authority#errors) lists the codes.

To hand the role to a different keyholder or a PDA, initialise first and then call `admin_transfer`, or nominate a successor, see [Hand over in two steps](#hand-over-in-two-steps).

## Fix the first admin at build time

Set `SPEL_ADMIN_GENESIS` to an account id, as 64 hex characters, when the program is built, and only that account can run `admin_initialize`. Anyone else is rejected with program error 6115, `signer is not this build's genesis admin`, which closes the initialisation window. Put it in a `.cargo/config.toml` in the project root, where every build picks it up:

```toml
[env]
SPEL_ADMIN_GENESIS = "<64 hex characters>"
```

The key is compiled into the program, so the program id changes with it. Compare `spel program-id` with and without the key to confirm it is in. A malformed or all-zero value fails the build. In embedded mode there is no `admin_initialize`: call `admin_authority::require_genesis(&caller)?` in your account-creating instruction for the same check.

## Transfer admin to another party

`admin_transfer` requires the current admin to sign. It takes an `AdminCandidate` describing the new admin, paired with a matching `AccountWithMetadata` that proves the candidate on chain.

Two candidate shapes:

```rust
// `AdminCandidate` is a re-exported alias for the shared authority type:
// `pub type AdminCandidate = AuthorityCandidate;`
pub enum AuthorityCandidate {
    /// The new admin is a keyholder. Validated by checking the new account
    /// co-signed the transaction.
    Signer,
    /// The new admin is a program-owned PDA. Validated by deriving the address
    /// from (program_id, seed) and confirming the PDA exists on chain.
    Pda { program_id: ProgramId, seed: [u8; 32] },
}
```

```bash
spel --idl program-idl.json --program <program-id> -- \
    admin-transfer \
    --caller <current-admin-account-id> \
    --new-account <new-admin-account-id> \
    --candidate Signer
```

A `Signer` transfer needs the new admin's signature on the same transaction, which proves the keyholder consents. That means two parties sign one message. Run as written, the command above builds and submits with the caller's signature only, and the sequencer drops the transaction unless the candidate's signature is attached. The `spel` CLI collects that second signature through a partial-transaction file ([logos-co/spel#246](https://github.com/logos-co/spel/pull/246)). The current admin adds the global flags `--co-signer` and `--export` before the `--` separator, which writes the transaction to a file instead of submitting it. The new admin signs it in their own wallet, offline, and anyone with a node connection submits it:

```bash
spel --co-signer <new-admin-account-id> --export handover.json \
    --idl program-idl.json --program <program-id> -- \
    admin-transfer \
    --caller <current-admin-account-id> \
    --new-account <new-admin-account-id> \
    --candidate Signer

# The new admin, in their own wallet:
spel sign handover.json

# Anyone with a node connection:
spel submit handover.json
```

`spel sign` prints the decoded instruction and asks for confirmation before it adds the signature. The file records the next `nonce` of both keys, so neither key may send another transaction between the export and the submit, otherwise the sequencer rejects the transfer. The new admin key needs a program owner, like the first admin's. The witness exchange section of the CLI README describes the file format.

After the transaction lands, the previous admin can no longer call gated instructions.

## Hand over in two steps

`admin_nominate` and `admin_accept` move the role without both parties signing one transaction. The current admin names the next admin, and the nominee later accepts on their own signature:

```bash
spel --idl program-idl.json --program <program-id> -- \
    admin-nominate --caller <current-admin-account-id> --new-admin <nominee-account-id-hex>

spel --idl program-idl.json --program <program-id> -- \
    admin-accept --caller <nominee-account-id>
```

`--new-admin` is a raw 32 byte argument, pass the account id as 64 hex characters, not the base58 form the wallet prints. Convert a base58 id with:

```bash
python3 -c 'import sys,functools;a="123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz";print(functools.reduce(lambda n,c:n*58+a.index(c),sys.argv[1],0).to_bytes(32,"big").hex())' <account-id>
```

Nothing changes until the nominee accepts, so a wrong id only costs a second nomination. A later nomination replaces an earlier one, nominating the all-zero id cancels, and `admin_transfer` and `admin_renounce` both clear a pending nominee. The nominee key needs a program owner. A PDA nominee accepts through its owning program, which chained-calls `admin_accept` with the seeds of the PDA.

## Use a program (PDA) as the admin

To delegate admin authority to another program, for example a multisig, use `AdminCandidate::Pda` with the delegating program's ID and PDA seed. Payload variants are passed to the CLI as a one-key JSON object:

```bash
spel --idl program-idl.json --program <program-id> -- \
    admin-transfer \
    --caller <current-admin-account-id> \
    --new-account <pda-account-id> \
    --candidate '{"Pda": {"program_id": "<multisig-program-id>", "seed": "<32-byte-hex-seed>"}}'
```

The PDA must already exist on chain as a claimed account, an unclaimed candidate is rejected. When the multisig later wants to invoke a gated instruction on your program, it does so through a chained call and declares its admin PDA in `caller-pda-seeds`. LEZ verifies the seed and propagates `is_authorized = true` to your program; the `#[require_admin]` check then accepts the PDA as the legitimate admin. No private key is needed for the PDA, authorisation comes from the seed delegation.

## Embedded mode, the admin slot inside your own account

Instead of a dedicated Config PDA, the admin slot can live inside one of your program's own accounts at a byte offset. Declared once, program wide, on the marker:

```rust
use admin_authority::AdminConfig;

#[account_type]
#[derive(BorshSerialize, BorshDeserialize, Clone, Debug)]
pub struct ProgramConfig {
    pub value: u64,           // bytes 0..8
    pub padding: [u8; 24],    // bytes 8..32
    #[admin_slot]
    pub admin: AdminConfig,   // bytes 32..96, the embedded slot
}

#[lez_program]
#[admin_authority(admin_config = config, offset = 32)]
mod my_program {
    use admin_authority::admin_initialize;

    #[admin_initialize]
    #[instruction]
    pub fn initialize(
        #[account(init, pda = literal("program_config"))] mut config: AccountWithMetadata,
    ) -> SpelResult {
        ProgramConfig {
            value: 0,
            padding: [0; 24],
            admin: AdminConfig::default(),
        }
        .write_to(&mut config)?;
        // the signing caller is injected, and the injected bootstrap
        // installs it as admin in this same transaction
        Ok(SpelOutput::execute(vec![config], vec![]))
    }
}
```

`write_to` is the same helper pattern from the gating section, implemented on `ProgramConfig`.

What changes:

- **No `admin_initialize` instruction.** Mark your own account-creating instruction with `#[admin_initialize]` instead. The bootstrap is injected, the caller is installed as admin in the same transaction that creates the account, and the slot is born initialised, so the initialisation window from the warning above does not exist in embedded mode. An account created without the bootstrap is born renounced, permanently.
- **`#[admin_slot]` keeps the layout honest.** The field marker derives an `ADMIN_SLOT_OFFSET` const and a layout test, and the build fails if the marker position and the `offset = ...` declaration ever disagree, for example after a field is added above the slot.
- **Everything retargets.** Gates read the slot at the declared offset from your account, the management instructions splice only the 64 byte window and leave your neighbouring fields untouched, and the IDL shows your account wherever the dedicated PDA used to appear.
- **The offset is never in a transaction.** It compiles into the program as a literal. The IDL carries no offset argument, and writing `admin_config = ...` or `offset = ...` on a gate by hand is a compile error in embedded mode.
- **One account fewer** on every gated transaction, the slot travels with state you were already passing.

The embedded `AdminConfig` field must sit at the declared offset with only fixed-size fields before it. The library repository ships a reference sample (`admin-authority-sample-embedded`) with the layout, tests, and a committed dry-run walkthrough.

## Renounce admin permanently

```bash
spel --idl program-idl.json --program <program-id> -- \
    admin-renounce --caller <current-admin-account-id>
```

This writes `AccountId::default()` to the Config PDA and clears any pending nominee. From then on every admin-gated instruction, `admin_transfer`, `admin_nominate` and `admin_accept` reject with program error 6102, `admin authority renounced`. There is no recovery path, design your program so renounce is only callable when permanent loss of mutability is the intended outcome (handoff to "immutable" governance, end of life, etc.).

## Verify your integration
